title: The King of the Jews Crucified
summary: At dawn the council hands Jesus over to Pontius Pilate, who, pressed by the chief priests and the crowd, releases the rebel Barabbas and sentences Jesus to be crucified. Soldiers mock him as king, Simon of Cyrene carries his cross, and he is crucified at Golgotha between two robbers under a charge that reads THE KING OF THE JEWS. After three hours of darkness he cries out in the words of Psalm 22 and dies; the temple curtain is torn, a Roman centurion confesses him as the Son of God, and Joseph of Arimathea buries him in a rock tomb while women watch.
story:
This is the climax of Mark's Gospel. The book's first line called Jesus the Christ and the Son of God (1:1), and throughout the story unclean spirits have known it while human beings struggled to see it. At the moment of his death a Gentile soldier says it. Every clause of the third passion prediction is now fulfilled: the Son of Man has been handed over to the chief priests, condemned, handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, spat on, flogged, and killed (10:33-34). His disciples have fled; only women watch, from a distance.

The chapter shows the kingship of Jesus in the most unlikely form. The title King of the Jews, never used in Mark before this chapter, is spoken by Pilate, shouted in mockery by soldiers, written on the charge above his head, and twisted by the priests into ‘King of Israel’. He is crowned with thorns, robed in purple, saluted, and enthroned on a cross with a bandit at his right and another at his left, the places James and John had asked for in his glory (10:37). The chapter moves by the clock: dawn (verse 1), the third hour (25), the sixth (33), the ninth (34), and evening (42), so that the reader walks through the day with him. Its last scene prepares for the next chapter. The death is certain, confirmed by a Roman officer; the body is buried; the stone is rolled against the tomb; and two women see where he is laid.
historical:
Pontius Pilate governed Judea as prefect from about AD 26 to 36. A limestone block found in 1961 by an Italian team led by Antonio Frova in the theater at Caesarea Maritima, where it had been reused in a later stairway, records his dedication of a building called the Tiberieum and gives his title as praefectus Iudaeae; the stone is now in the Israel Museum. The Jewish writers Philo and Josephus describe him as harsh and provocative. Philo quotes a letter of Herod Agrippa I charging him with insults, robberies, and executions without trial, and tells how he set up gilded shields in Herod's palace in Jerusalem (Embassy to Gaius 299-305). Josephus tells of his bringing military standards bearing the emperor's image into Jerusalem, of his use of temple funds for an aqueduct and the violent suppression of the protest that followed, and of an attack on Samaritans that led to his recall to Rome around 36 or 37 (Jewish War 2.169-177; Antiquities 18.55-62, 85-89). Luke 13:1 mentions Galileans whose blood Pilate mingled with their sacrifices. The Roman historian Tacitus, writing around 116, records that Christus, from whom the Christians took their name, suffered the extreme penalty in the reign of Tiberius at the hands of the procurator Pontius Pilate (Annals 15.44), and Josephus's paragraph on Jesus (Antiquities 18.63-64), though later expanded by Christian copyists, is widely thought to have said in its original form that Pilate condemned him to the cross.

Because the council could not carry out a death sentence (John 18:31), it brought Jesus to Pilate on a charge Rome would care about: claiming to be King of the Jews, which amounted to rebellion against Caesar. Barabbas had been imprisoned with rebels who had committed murder ‘during the insurrection’, one of many disturbances under Pilate that the sources mention only in part. The Passover amnesty is known only from the Gospels, but indirect evidence makes it plausible: the Mishnah allows a Passover lamb to be slaughtered for someone the authorities have promised to release from prison (m. Pesachim 8:6), and a papyrus from Egypt dated AD 85 records a governor handing a prisoner over to the crowd (Papyrus Florence 61).

Crucifixion was the Roman punishment for slaves, violent criminals, and rebels, designed to be slow, public, and shameful. Cicero called it the most cruel and disgusting penalty (Against Verres 2.5.165). The governor of Syria, Varus, crucified two thousand Jewish rebels after the disturbances that followed Herod's death in 4 BC (Josephus, Antiquities 17.295), and during the siege of AD 70 Titus's soldiers crucified up to five hundred captured Jews a day before the walls, nailing them in different postures for sport (Jewish War 5.449-451). Victims were flogged, made to carry the crossbeam, and nailed or tied to the cross, often dying over many hours of exhaustion and suffocation. In 1968 an ossuary found at Giv'at ha-Mivtar in north Jerusalem held the heel bone of a man named Yehohanan with an iron nail still through it, published in 1970, the only skeletal evidence of crucifixion from Roman Judea; it shows both that victims were nailed and that a crucified man could be buried in a family tomb. The law required that the body of an executed man not remain hanging overnight (Deuteronomy 21:22-23), and Josephus notes that Jews took down and buried even the crucified before sunset (Jewish War 4.317). The traditional site of the crucifixion and burial was enclosed in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, built under Constantine and dedicated in 335 (Eusebius, Life of Constantine book 3); excavations show the area was a disused quarry with rock-cut tombs, outside the city wall in Jesus' day.
cultural:
Roman soldiers' mockery parodied a royal investiture. Purple was the color of kings and emperors; the twisted thorns imitated the wreath of a victor or the radiate crown of a ruler; ‘Hail, King of the Jews’ mimicked the salute to the emperor; kneeling and bowing was the homage owed to a monarch. Philo describes a crowd in Alexandria in AD 38 mocking the Jewish king Agrippa by dressing a harmless madman named Carabas with a papyrus crown and a mat for a robe and saluting him as lord (Against Flaccus 36-39), which shows how such scenes were staged. The Praetorium was the governor's headquarters in Jerusalem, most likely Herod's former palace on the city's western side, though an older tradition places it at the Antonia fortress beside the temple, where the Via Dolorosa begins. Mark explains the Greek word aulē with the Latin praetorium and uses more Latin loanwords than any other Gospel (legion, denarius, centurion, speculator, flagellate), one reason many scholars link the book with Rome.

Cyrene was a Greek city in North Africa (modern Libya) with a large Jewish community; Cyrenian Jews had a synagogue in Jerusalem (Acts 6:9). The Roman right of requisition, angaria, allowed soldiers to press a civilian into service (compare Matthew 5:41). Mark names Simon's sons Alexander and Rufus as if his readers knew them; a burial cave in the Kidron Valley excavated in 1941 held ossuaries of a family from Cyrene, one inscribed ‘Alexander son of Simon’, and a Rufus is greeted in Romans 16:13, though both names were common. Golgotha is Aramaic for ‘skull’. The Babylonian Talmud records that a man led out to execution was given frankincense in wine to dull his senses, provided by respected women of Jerusalem (b. Sanhedrin 43a, citing Proverbs 31:6); Mark's wine mixed with myrrh may be such a drink, and Jesus refuses it. The clothes of the executed were the soldiers' perquisite. A placard naming the crime was often carried before the condemned or fixed to the cross (Suetonius, Caligula 32; Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 5.1.44).

Mark counts the hours from sunrise: the third hour about 9 a.m., the sixth noon, the ninth 3 p.m., the hour of the afternoon sacrifice and prayer in the temple (Acts 3:1). Elijah, who had not died but was taken up (2 Kings 2:11), was expected to come before the day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5), and popular belief pictured him as a helper of the righteous in distress, which explains the bystanders' taunt. Sour wine (oxos), a cheap vinegary wine diluted with water, was the ordinary drink of soldiers and laborers. The temple had two great curtains, an outer one before the sanctuary doors and an inner one before the Holy of Holies, which only the high priest entered, once a year on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16); Josephus describes the outer curtain as a Babylonian woven hanging of blue, scarlet, linen, and purple depicting the heavens (Jewish War 5.212-214). A centurion commanded a century of about eighty men. In the imperial world ‘son of god’ was a title of the emperor, since Augustus called himself divi filius, son of the deified Julius, on his coins. Preparation day (paraskeuē) was Friday, the day to prepare for the Sabbath, which began at sunset. Wealthier families buried their dead in tombs cut into the limestone, laying the body on a bench and later gathering the bones into an ossuary; most were closed with a squared blocking stone, a few with a round rolling stone.
literary:
Mark tells the crucifixion with restraint. The act itself takes three Greek words in verse 24, ‘and they crucify him’, and he says almost nothing about the physical suffering. Instead he lets irony carry the meaning. Every mockery speaks the truth. Jesus is the King of the Jews; he did save others, and he cannot save himself if he is to finish saving them; he will build the temple not made with hands in three days in a way his mockers do not imagine. The title King appears six times (verses 2, 9, 12, 18, 26, 32), and the three groups of mockers, passersby (29 and 30), chief priests and scribes (31 and 32), and the men crucified with him (32), echo the three questions of the trials. The priests' demand to ‘see and believe’ reverses Mark's order, in which faith comes before sight.

Psalm 22, the lament of a righteous sufferer, runs through the account: the dividing of garments (Psalm 22:18, verse 24), the wagging heads (22:7, verse 29), and the cry of forsakenness (22:1, verse 34), which Mark gives first in Aramaic and then translates. Psalm 69's sour wine (69:21) is echoed in verse 36. The darkness from noon to three recalls the ninth plague on Egypt just before the first Passover (Exodus 10:21-23) and Amos 8:9, where God makes the sun go down at noon in judgment. Mark's day is structured by three-hour steps, and the hours match the watches of 13:35.

The climax brings together the chapter's threads in a single sentence and its answer. Jesus cries out and breathes his last, exepneusen, a verb built on the root of pneuma, spirit or breath. The curtain of the temple is torn, eschisthē, the verb Mark used for the heavens ‘breaking open’ at the baptism (1:10), when the Spirit came down and the voice named him Son. At both tearings Jesus is named Son of God, first by the Father and now by a centurion, and David Ulansey (Journal of Biblical Literature, 1991) argued that Josephus's description of the outer curtain as a picture of the heavens makes the frame deliberate. The Gospel that began with the heavens torn ends its account of Jesus' life with the curtain torn. The last paragraphs return to the women, named in verse 40 and again in verse 47, whose watching links death, burial, and empty tomb. Verse 28, absent from the earliest manuscripts, is discussed under the text.

outline.t: Darkness, the cry, the death, the torn curtain, the confession
The women watching from a distance

doctrines.note: The innocent Jesus is condemned while Barabbas, a murderer, goes free (verse 15), a picture of substitution the church has seen at the heart of the cross. His cry of forsakenness shows him entering the separation from God that sin brings (compare 2 Corinthians 5:21, Galatians 3:13), and the curtain torn at his death declares that the way into God's presence is open. Christians confess that he died for sinners, bearing their judgment.

Mark makes Jesus' kingship the charge, the mockery, and the truth. He is crowned with thorns, saluted in scorn, lifted up under the title THE KING OF THE JEWS, and taunted as ‘the Christ, the King of Israel’ (verse 32). God's anointed king is revealed not by escaping the cross but by his faithfulness on it, and the first human confession of him as Son of God comes at his death (verse 39).

The veil of the temple is torn from top to bottom at the moment of Jesus' death (verse 38), a tearing from God's side. Whether the outer or inner curtain is meant, the sign speaks both of judgment on the temple, as Jesus foretold (13:2), and of access to God opened through his death, as Hebrews 10:19-20 develops.

Jesus prays the opening line of Psalm 22 in his agony: “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” (verse 34). The righteous sufferer of Israel's laments finds his fullest expression in him. Those who suffer and feel abandoned can pray the same words, knowing that Christ prayed them first, still addressing God as ‘my God’, and that the psalm ends in vindication.

Joseph of Arimathea ‘was waiting for the kingdom of God’ (verse 43) at the moment the King lay dead. The chapter shows the kingdom Jesus announced in 1:15 arriving by the road of rejection and death, and Joseph's courageous act of hope is rewarded two days later.

words.note: Stauroō, to crucify, from stauros, an upright stake or cross. It occurs about forty-six times in the New Testament and eight in Mark, seven of them in this chapter, from the crowd's shout (verses 13 and 14) and Pilate's sentence (15) to the soldiers' act (20, 24, 25, 27); verse 32 uses a compound for the men crucified with him. To the Roman world it named the most shameful of deaths, reserved for slaves and rebels; Paul makes ‘Christ crucified’ the center of his preaching (1 Corinthians 1:23, 2:2), and the young man at the tomb will call the risen Jesus ‘the crucified one’ (16:6).

Basileus, king. It occurs about 115 times in the New Testament and twelve in Mark, six of them in this chapter (verses 2, 9, 12, 18, 26, 32). In Mark the phrase King of the Jews is a Gentile's phrase, used by Pilate, the soldiers, and the Roman placard; the Jewish leaders say King of Israel, Israel's own name for itself. Rome meant the title as a charge of sedition; Mark means it as the truth about Jesus, spoken by those who do not believe it.

Sōzō, to save, rescue, heal. It occurs about 107 times in the New Testament and fifteen in Mark, where it is used both for physical healing (5:34, 10:52) and for final salvation (8:35, 13:13). In this chapter it appears three times on the lips of mockers: ‘save Yourself’ (verse 30) and ‘He saved others, but He cannot save Himself’ (31). The irony is complete. Jesus had said that whoever wants to save his life will lose it (8:35), and he saves others precisely by refusing to save himself.

Empaizō, to mock, ridicule, make sport of. It occurs thirteen times in the New Testament, all in the first three Gospels, and almost every use belongs to the passion story or its predictions. Jesus used it in the third passion prediction (10:34), and Mark uses it twice here, of the soldiers (verse 20) and of the priests (31). The verb describes treating a person as a plaything; Mark shows the King of the Jews treated as a joke by Gentile soldiers and Jewish leaders alike.

Egkataleipō, to forsake, abandon, leave behind utterly. It occurs about ten times in the New Testament, including Hebrews 13:5, where God says he will never forsake his people, and 2 Corinthians 4:9, ‘struck down but not forsaken’. In verse 34 it translates the Aramaic shebaqtani and follows the Greek of Psalm 22:1. The aorist presents the forsakenness as something that has happened, not only a feeling. The church has read it as the Son bearing the weight of sin's judgment, while never teaching that the Trinity was divided in its being.

Katapetasma, curtain or veil. It occurs six times in the New Testament: in the three accounts of Jesus' death (Matthew 27:51, Mark 15:38, Luke 23:45) and three times in Hebrews (6:19, 9:3, 10:20). In the Greek Old Testament it names both the curtain before the Most Holy Place (Exodus 26:31-33) and the screen at the entrance of the tent. Hebrews develops the image of the inner curtain: believers enter the holy places ‘through the curtain, that is, through His flesh’ (Hebrews 10:20).

Huios, son. It occurs about 379 times in the New Testament and about thirty-five in Mark. The title Son of God frames the Gospel: the first line (1:1), the Father's voice at the baptism (1:11) and transfiguration (9:7), the cries of unclean spirits (3:11, 5:7), the high priest's question (14:61), and now the centurion (verse 39). His phrase has no article, huios theou, and grammarians debate whether a pagan soldier meant ‘a son of God’ or ‘the Son of God’; in Mark's story it is the confession the whole book has been waiting for, spoken at last by a human being.

christ:
Here Mark shows most clearly who Jesus is and what he has done. He is the King of the Jews, crowned and robed in mockery, his throne a cross, his courtiers two bandits. He is the Son of Man who came not to be served but to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45), and here he gives it. He is the servant of Isaiah 53 who is silent before his accusers (verse 5; Isaiah 53:7), numbered with transgressors (verse 27; Isaiah 53:12), and cut off for the sin of others. He is the righteous sufferer of Psalm 22, mocked, stripped, his garments divided, crying out to a God who seems absent, and the psalm he begins ends with the ends of the earth turning to the LORD (Psalm 22:27), which begins at once when a Roman centurion confesses him.

The exchange with Barabbas, whose name means ‘son of the father’, sets the true Son of the Father in the place of a guilty man who walks free. The darkness at noon recalls the plague on Egypt before the first Passover and Amos's day of judgment, and Jesus dies at the Passover as the lamb Paul names him (1 Corinthians 5:7). The torn curtain says that his death achieves what the Day of Atonement pointed to (Hebrews 9:11-12, 10:19-20) and ends the old temple's role, as he foretold. And the centurion's confession, “Truly this man was the Son of God!”, gathers the whole Gospel: the Son is known not at a miracle but at the cross, in the manner of his dying. Mark says the confession came “When the centurion standing there in front of Jesus saw how He had breathed His last” (verse 39).

The church confesses on the witness of this chapter that Jesus truly died. Pilate confirms it with the centurion, Joseph wraps the body, and the women see the tomb. That is the first-order confession of the creeds, that he was crucified under Pontius Pilate, suffered, died, and was buried, the one place a Roman governor's name enters the church's creed, fixing the gospel in datable history. It is also the ground of the next chapter. Because the death was real and witnessed, the empty tomb is news.
interpretation:
Christian reading of the crucifixion began with the Old Testament texts Mark wove into it. The earliest surviving Christian sermon on the Passover, Melito of Sardis's On the Pascha (around 160 to 170), read the cross through the exodus with great power, and also first charged Israel with killing God, a line that later centuries used to justify contempt and violence against Jews. The second-century Gospel of Peter retold the scene with Herod rather than Pilate giving the order and rendered the cry of verse 34 ‘My power, my power, you have abandoned me’. Pagan critics mocked a crucified God: a graffito scratched on a wall near the Palatine in Rome around 200, the earliest known picture of the crucifixion, shows a man worshiping a crucified figure with a donkey's head. Augustine, in his Expositions of the Psalms on Psalm 22 (21 in his Latin), taught that Christ on the cross spoke as ‘the whole Christ’, head and body together, voicing the forsakenness of the humanity he had taken on, a reading that shaped the medieval West.

The cross became the center of Western theology of salvation. Anselm of Canterbury's Why God Became Man (Cur Deus Homo, 1098) argued that the God-man's death rendered the satisfaction humanity owed. Luther's Heidelberg Disputation (1518) set a theology of the cross, which finds God hidden in suffering and shame, against a theology of glory. Calvin (Institutes 2.16.10-12) read the cry of forsakenness as the core of the creed's ‘he descended into hell’: on the cross Christ endured in his soul the dread of a man forsaken by God. Hermann Samuel Reimarus, in fragments Lessing published between 1774 and 1778, took the same cry as evidence that Jesus died disappointed in his hope of an earthly kingdom, opening the modern quest for the historical Jesus. Jürgen Moltmann's The Crucified God (1972, English 1974) made the cry the starting point of his theology and drew on Elie Wiesel's account in Night of a boy hanged at Auschwitz. Martin Hengel's Crucifixion (English 1977) documented how shameful the death was in the ancient world. Jewish scholars from Joseph Klausner (1922) onward read the trial and death of Jesus as a Jewish story under Roman rule, and the Second Vatican Council's Nostra Aetate (1965) rejected the charge that the Jewish people as a whole bore guilt for the crucifixion. Midrash Tehillim, a Jewish commentary on the Psalms, reads Psalm 22 as the prayer of Queen Esther in her danger, a reminder that the psalm had a life of its own in Jewish devotion.

The chapter fills the church's worship. Mark 15 is part of the Passion Gospel for Palm Sunday in Year B of the Revised Common Lectionary and the Roman lectionary, and both allow a shorter reading beginning at 15:1. The Stations of the Cross, the Tenebrae services of Holy Week, and the devotion of the Seven Last Words gather the chapter's scenes; Joseph Haydn wrote his orchestral Seven Last Words of Our Saviour on the Cross for Good Friday in Cádiz, first performed in 1787. The medieval hymn Salve caput cruentatum, probably by the Cistercian abbot Arnulf of Leuven in the thirteenth century, meditates on the thorn-crowned head of verse 17; Paul Gerhardt's German version, O Haupt voll Blut und Wunden (1656), became the chorale that runs through Bach's St Matthew Passion and, in English, ‘O Sacred Head, Now Wounded’.
text:
English Bibles differ at several points in this chapter.

Verse 28 is the most visible. The King James Version reads ‘And the scripture was fulfilled, which saith, And he was numbered with the transgressors’. The words are absent from the oldest manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Bezae) and present in later ones, including the Byzantine text. They quote Isaiah 53:12, which Jesus applies to himself in Luke 22:37, and were almost certainly added from there; Mark rarely adds fulfillment formulas of his own. Modern Bibles put the verse in a footnote, which is why their numbering skips from 27 to 29.

In verse 8 most early manuscripts, including the first hand of Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, read that the crowd ‘went up’ (anabas), while Alexandrinus, Washingtonianus, and the Byzantine text read ‘crying aloud’ (anaboēsas), the reading behind the King James Version; the two Greek words look and sound alike. In verse 12 some manuscripts lack ‘the One you call’, which makes Pilate's question flatter. In verse 34 Codex Bezae and some Old Latin manuscripts read ‘why have you reproached me’ instead of ‘why have you forsaken me’; Bart Ehrman (The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture, 1993) argued that the change softened a cry some found hard to reconcile with Jesus' divinity. In verse 39 many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add that the centurion saw that Jesus ‘so cried out’ and breathed his last; the earliest lack the words. In verses 40 and 47 the name of Mary's son varies between Joses and Joseph in the manuscripts, which is why some English Bibles differ.

One apparent conflict is with John rather than within Mark's text. Mark places the crucifixion at the third hour (verse 25), about 9 a.m., while John says Pilate was still judging Jesus at about the sixth hour (John 19:14). A few manuscripts of each Gospel changed the number to match the other, and interpreters since Eusebius have proposed a copying error, rough reckoning in three-hour blocks, or different theological purposes.

teach.big: At the cross the rejected King of the Jews gives his life in the place of the guilty, enters the full darkness of forsakenness, and by his death opens the way to God, so that the first human being to confess him as Son of God is a Gentile executioner.

outline.t: Jesus is handed from one authority to the next, and his silence before false charges is not weakness but the servant's freedom; he does not defend himself because he has come to give himself.
Everyone shares the guilt: priests acting from envy, a crowd that chooses a murderer, a judge who knows better and gives in, and Barabbas, the guilty man who goes free because Jesus is condemned.
The soldiers stage a coronation as a joke, and every detail tells the truth: this is the King, and this is how he reigns.
He is crucified between bandits and mocked by every group, and the taunt is Mark's gospel in reverse: he saves others precisely by not saving himself.
In the darkness Jesus prays Scripture's cry of abandonment, dies, and in that moment the curtain is torn and a Gentile sees who he is: the Son of God is known at the cross.
When the men have fled, women who followed and served him in Galilee stay and watch, faithful witnesses the world discounted.
A council member risks his standing to bury Jesus, Pilate confirms the death, and the women mark the tomb: the death is real, so Easter will be news.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misuses are common. The first and most harmful is to use this chapter to blame the Jewish people. The crowd before Pilate was one gathering in one city, stirred up by particular leaders, and a Roman governor passed the sentence that Roman soldiers carried out. Mark's own framing places everyone inside the guilt, and the church has confessed that sinners, including Christians, are the authors of Christ's sufferings. The second is to dwell on the physical horror of crucifixion in ways the text does not. Mark says almost nothing of the pain; he points to its meaning, and preaching that competes with film in gore can miss the irony, the Scripture, and the confession that carry the chapter.

A third error flattens the cry of verse 34, either by insisting that Jesus only quoted the psalm's first line to recall its happy ending, or by describing the Father's rejection of the Son in terms that divide the Trinity. The text allows the cry its full force and still has Jesus say ‘my God’. A fourth is to read Pilate as either a pure villain or a sympathetic victim of the crowd; the historical Pilate was harsh, and Mark shows him managing a crowd to protect himself. Finally, avoid treating the centurion's words as a fully formed creed. Whatever he meant, Mark presents them as the true confession, and the teacher's task is to show why the manner of Jesus' death, not a miracle, produced it.
teach.pastoral: This chapter presses on people who feel abandoned by God, and on those who have suffered injustice or public shame. Verse 34 gives them words Jesus himself prayed: a believer can ask God ‘why’ and still call him ‘my God’. Do not hurry past that cry to a tidy answer; many in the room need permission to lament. The chapter also speaks to victims of violence and abuse. Jesus was stripped, beaten, spat on, and mocked by people with power over him, and teachers should name that plainly without suggesting that suffering abuse is itself a virtue or that victims should accept it. For those who feel they have failed Jesus as the disciples did, the women who stayed and the councilor who risked his reputation show that faithfulness can begin late and small. And for anyone near death or grieving, the burial is a comfort: Jesus went all the way into the grave, and the ones who love him know where he was laid.

hard.q: When Jesus cried, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” was he truly abandoned by God?
hard.a:
The cry raises two objections of opposite kinds. The skeptical form was put by Hermann Samuel Reimarus, whose fragments Lessing published in the 1770s: the cry shows that Jesus had hoped for God to establish his kingdom and died realizing God had not helped him, so the Christian story of a planned sacrifice was invented afterward. Many modern critics hear in the verse the despair of a failed prophet. The theological form asks how the Father could forsake the Son if the Trinity is one God, and whether speaking of abandonment divides what cannot be divided. Jewish readers add that Psalm 22 has its own history, read in the rabbinic Midrash Tehillim as the prayer of Esther in danger, and that Christian use of it can erase the psalm's meaning for Israel.

Christian responses fall into several families. One stresses that Jesus prays Scripture, and that a psalm's first line could call the whole to mind; Psalm 22 moves from lament to trust (22:21-24) and ends with God's rule proclaimed to all nations, so the cry is faith spoken from the depths, not despair. Raymond Brown (The Death of the Messiah, 1994) and many others insist that the first line must still be heard in its own force: Jesus experiences real abandonment and does not pretend otherwise. A second family, following Paul's statements that God made him who knew no sin to be sin for us and that Christ became a curse for us (2 Corinthians 5:21, Galatians 3:13), holds that Jesus bore the judgment due to sin, including the loss of the felt presence of God; Calvin (Institutes 2.16.10-12) read the creed's ‘descended into hell’ this way. A third, from Augustine's Expositions of the Psalms, holds that Christ spoke in the person of the humanity he had joined to himself, voicing our forsakenness rather than his own. Theologians across traditions agree that the eternal union of Father and Son was not broken; the Son still calls on ‘my God’. Jürgen Moltmann went further, speaking of a rupture within God's own experience, a proposal other theologians judge to go beyond the text. The cry is real anguish, voiced in Scripture's words, by one who entered the full darkness of human abandonment; how best to describe what the Son experienced is a question on which faithful interpreters differ.

hard.q: Does Mark shift the blame for Jesus' death from Rome to the Jewish leaders and people?
hard.a:
The objection is serious and has a history of real harm. Crucifixion was a Roman punishment, carried out by Roman soldiers on a Roman governor's order, for a Roman charge of sedition. Yet Mark shows Pilate hesitating, knowing Jesus is innocent, and yielding to priests and a crowd. Philo and Josephus describe a Pilate who was harsh and contemptuous of Jewish opinion, not one who could be pushed around. Jewish scholars such as Joseph Klausner, Paul Winter (On the Trial of Jesus, 1961), and Haim Cohn argued that the Gospels, written after the war with Rome for readers in the empire, softened Rome's role and enlarged the role of the Jewish authorities. John Dominic Crossan (Who Killed Jesus?, 1995) argued that the passion narratives were shaped by later conflicts between church and synagogue. The results were grievous. Melito of Sardis, in the second century, already accused Israel of killing God, and the charge of deicide fed centuries of Christian contempt and violence against Jews.

Responses come from several directions. Helen Bond (Pontius Pilate in History and Interpretation, 1998) argued that Mark's Pilate is not weak but a shrewd politician who manipulates a crowd to have his way, which fits the harsh governor of Philo and Josephus. Raymond Brown (The Death of the Messiah, 1994) concluded that some Jerusalem authorities did take part in handing Jesus over, as Josephus's paragraph on Jesus also says, while the decision and the execution were Roman. Many point out that Mark names particular groups, the chief priests, elders, and scribes, not the Jewish people, that the crowd before Pilate was a small gathering stirred up by those leaders, and that the Twelve, all of them Jews, share the guilt of desertion. The church's own confession runs against the misuse: the Roman Catechism (1566) taught that sinners of every age are the authors of Christ's sufferings, and Christians more than others; Acts 4:27 gathers Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles, and the peoples of Israel together; and the Second Vatican Council's Nostra Aetate (1965) stated that the passion cannot be charged against all Jews then living or against Jews today. How much the Gospels shaped their accounts for Roman readers remains debated among historians; that the chapter gives no warrant for blaming the Jewish people is not.

interpret: How is the taunt ‘He saved others, but He cannot save Himself’ both false and true?

Why might Mark make a Roman centurion, rather than a disciple, the first human being to call Jesus the Son of God?
apply: Barabbas, guilty, went free while Jesus, innocent, was crucified. How does it change your view of the cross to see yourself in Barabbas's place?
The women watched from a distance when the disciples had fled. What does faithfulness look like when you cannot change what is happening but can still stay?
